newsitem.title: BRAZIL: Brazil begins to cut federal payroll.
newsitem.headline: Brazil begins to cut federal payroll.

text.p: The Brazilian government extinguished about 25,600 vacant posts in the federal administration on Monday as part of a cost-cutting plan, Claudia Costin, the Administration Ministry's executive secretary, said.
A further 72,900 jobs which are currently occupied will be phased out over the next five to eight years as their current occupants gradually retire, Costin told reporters.
The job cuts were announced Friday as part of a wide-ranging package of measures to cut costs in the federal government and raise more tax revenues.

Also effective Monday were a ban on overtime, raises for civil servants substituting for their superiors and a rule that public sector workers may not rejoin the civil service as full employees once they have retired from a previous federal post.
Costin said the government was still working on the final details of a voluntary retirment program which, she said, should be completed by March 1997.
While declining to estimate how many civil servants the government hoped might join the program, Costin said the ministry's highest possible figure was about 40,000.
"But we'll never get that many," she said.

Once the voluntary retirement program were finished, the government would begin to relocate workers to avoid imbalances between sectors and establish programs to reward workers on a performance basis, Costin said.

The goverment was also working on a decree to compensate civil servants who might be fired because they did not take entrance examinations and did not qualify for the public sector's jobs-for-life guarantees, known as "stability," she said.
An estimated 55,000 of a total 570,000 federal civil servants are "unstable" and may be dismissed as part of the cost-cutting program.

A constitutional amendment awaiting its first, committee-level vote in Congress would enable all three levels of government to dismiss "stable" workers as long as their payroll spending exceeded 60 percent of receipts.
